entries.meaning: A place of higher education that grants degrees and does research. ---
examples: She teaches physics at a state university.
He applied to four universities in the Midwest.
The university raised its fees again this year.

entries.meaning: A school that students attend after high school to earn a degree. ---
examples: Their oldest son starts college in the fall.
She went to a small college in Ohio.
Both colleges offered him financial aid.
entries.contrast: In the US, college normally means four-year higher education, and Americans say went to college where the British say went to university.

entries.meaning: The first year of American school, for children about five years old. ---
examples: My daughter starts kindergarten in September.
He learned to write his name in kindergarten.
The two kindergartens share one playground.

entries.meaning: A school for children who are too young for kindergarten. ---
examples: We put him in preschool three mornings a week.
The preschool down the block has a waiting list.
Most preschools in town close at noon.

entries.meaning: An American school for children from about age five to eleven. ---
examples: She teaches fourth grade at an elementary school.
I walked to elementary school every morning.
The district closed two elementary schools last spring.

entries.meaning: An American school for students roughly between ages eleven and fourteen. ---
examples: My son is in middle school now.
Middle school was the hardest three years of my life.
The town has two middle schools and one high school.

entries.meaning: The last four years of American school, before college. ---
examples: We met in high school.
She graduated from high school in 2019.
The city's three high schools play each other every fall.

entries.meaning: A private school, or a school that trains people in one particular field. ---
examples: He spent two years at a military academy.
The riding academy takes students as young as six.
Several private academies opened downtown.

entries.meaning: A room in a school where lessons are taught. ---
examples: There are thirty desks in the classroom.
No food or drinks in the classroom, please.
The new building has twelve classrooms.

entries.meaning: A large room with rows of seats where a professor teaches many students at once. ---
examples: The lecture hall seats four hundred.
I sat in the back of the lecture hall and took notes.
Both lecture halls are being remodeled this summer.

entries.meaning: A large hall in a school where assemblies and performances are held. ---
examples: The whole school squeezed into the auditorium.
Graduation is held in the auditorium if it rains.
Both auditoriums need new sound systems.

entries.meaning: The large indoor room at a school used for sports and exercise classes. ---
examples: We have gym right after lunch.
The basketball game is in the school gym.
Both gyms were built in the seventies.

entries.meaning: An outdoor area at a school where children play during breaks. ---
examples: The kids ran out to the playground.
A teacher watches the playground at recess.
The city rebuilt three school playgrounds last year.

entries.meaning: A building or room holding books that people can read or borrow. ---
examples: I study in the library between classes.
The library closes at ten on weeknights.
Two campus libraries stay open all night during finals.

entries.meaning: A room fitted out for scientific experiments and testing. ---
examples: Safety goggles are required in the laboratory.
She works in a research laboratory on campus.
The chemistry laboratories are on the third floor.
entries.contrast: American stress falls on the first syllable, LAB-ruh-tor-ee; the British say luh-BOR-uh-tree. Americans usually shorten it to lab.

entries.meaning: A college building where students live. ---
examples: He lives in a dorm on the north side of campus.
The dorm has a laundry room in the basement.
Freshmen have to stay in the dorms their first year.

entries.meaning: A dark board on a classroom wall that you write on with chalk. ---
examples: She wrote the homework on the chalkboard.
Someone erased the chalkboard before class.
The old chalkboards were replaced with whiteboards.
entries.contrast: The l in chalk is silent: CHAWK-bord.

entries.meaning: A board on a wall where notices and announcements are pinned up. ---
examples: The class list is posted on the bulletin board.
Somebody stapled a flyer to the bulletin board.
The hallway bulletin boards are covered in club signs.
entries.contrast: American bulletin board; the British call it a notice board.

entries.meaning: A slip of paper that lets a student leave class and walk in the halls. ---
examples: You need a hall pass to go to the bathroom.
He forged a hall pass and got caught.
The teacher keeps the hall passes by the door.

entries.meaning: A room where people change clothes and store things before sports. ---
examples: Meet me in the locker room after practice.
The locker room smells like wet socks.
Both locker rooms were repainted over the summer.

entries.meaning: The class an American student reports to at the start of the day for attendance and announcements. ---
examples: Announcements are read during homeroom.
We were in the same homeroom all four years.
The homerooms meet for ten minutes each morning.

entries.meaning: A yellow bus that carries children to and from school. ---
examples: The school bus comes at seven fifteen.
He missed the school bus again.
You have to stop when school buses put their lights on.

entries.meaning: Someone who teaches a subject or skill, especially at a college. ---
examples: The instructor handed back our essays.
My driving instructor was very patient.
Two instructors share the same office.

entries.meaning: Someone who teaches one student or a few students privately. ---
examples: We hired a tutor to help him with algebra.
Her math tutor comes on Thursdays.
The writing center has free tutors.
entries.contrast: Americans say TOO-tur; the British say TYOO-tuh.

entries.meaning: Someone who gives talks to students at a college or university. ---
examples: The guest lecturer spoke for an hour.
He works as a part-time lecturer in history.
Several lecturers signed the letter.

entries.meaning: A senior official who runs a college or a division of a university. ---
examples: The dean approved my schedule change.
The dean wants to see you in her office.
All the deans met on Monday morning.

entries.meaning: Someone at a school who advises students about classes, colleges, and personal problems. ---
examples: My guidance counselor helped me pick a college.
Talk to a counselor if you're feeling overwhelmed.
The school hired two more counselors.
entries.contrast: American spelling has one l; the British write counsellor. Do not confuse it with councilor, a member of a council.

entries.meaning: Someone who is in the same class as you. ---
examples: A classmate lent me her notes.
He still keeps in touch with his old classmates.
My classmate sits right behind me.

entries.meaning: Someone you share a room or apartment with. ---
examples: My roommate studies until three in the morning.
He got a new roommate second semester.
The four roommates split the rent evenly.

entries.meaning: A student in the first year of high school or college. ---
examples: She's a freshman at the state university.
Freshmen move into the dorms a week early.
He was a freshman the year I was a senior.
entries.contrast: Irregular plural: one freshman, two freshmen.

entries.meaning: A student in the second year of high school or college. ---
examples: He made the varsity team as a sophomore.
The sophomores take chemistry this year.
Two sophomores joined the debate team.

entries.meaning: A student in the third year of high school or college. ---
examples: Juniors take the college entrance exam in the spring.
She's a junior majoring in biology.
Most of my friends are juniors.

entries.meaning: A student in the final year of high school or college. ---
examples: The seniors get out of class early on Fridays.
As a senior, he only needs three more credits.
Seniors have their own parking lot.

entries.meaning: Someone who has finished a course of study and received a degree or diploma. ---
examples: She's a graduate of a small liberal arts college.
Recent graduates are having trouble finding work.
The company hires graduates every June.
entries.contrast: The noun ends in an unstressed GRAJ-oo-uht; the verb to graduate ends in GRAJ-oo-ayt.

entries.meaning: A college student who has not yet earned a first degree. ---
examples: The class is open to undergraduates only.
As an undergraduate she worked in the campus bookstore.
Most undergraduates live within a mile of campus.

entries.meaning: Someone who studies a subject deeply and knows a great deal about it. ---
examples: He's a respected scholar of American history.
Scholars still argue about who wrote the letter.
The library invited a visiting scholar to speak.

entries.meaning: The student with the highest grades in a class, who gives a speech at graduation. ---
examples: She was the valedictorian of her high school class.
The valedictorian thanked her parents first.
Two students tied, so there were co-valedictorians.

entries.meaning: A teacher who fills in when the regular teacher is absent. ---
examples: We had a substitute in math all week.
The substitute let us watch a movie.
The district is short on substitutes this winter.

entries.meaning: The official in charge of all the public schools in an American district. ---
examples: The superintendent canceled school because of the snow.
Parents complained to the superintendent.
Three superintendents have come and gone in five years.

entries.meaning: A teacher who helps a student choose classes and plan a degree. ---
examples: I have to meet with my advisor before I register.
Her thesis advisor read three drafts.
The department assigns advisors to new students.

entries.meaning: Someone who leaves school before finishing. ---
examples: He was a high school dropout who later got his diploma.
The school is trying to bring dropouts back.
Many dropouts come back and finish years later.

entries.meaning: The study of numbers, shapes, and calculation. ---
examples: I have math first period.
She's always been good at math.
There's a lot of math in that class.
entries.contrast: Americans say math; the British say maths.

entries.meaning: The branch of math that uses letters to stand for unknown numbers. ---
examples: We start algebra in eighth grade.
He failed algebra and had to take it again.
Algebra finally made sense to me in college.

entries.meaning: The branch of math that deals with lines, angles, and shapes. ---
examples: Geometry was my favorite class.
You need a protractor for geometry.
She's teaching geometry to sophomores this year.

entries.meaning: The branch of math dealing with triangles and the ratios of their sides. ---
examples: Trigonometry comes after geometry at our school.
You can't do physics without some trigonometry.
He's tutoring her in trigonometry.

entries.meaning: The science of living things. ---
examples: We dissected a frog in biology.
She majored in biology and went to medical school.
Biology meets in the lab on Tuesdays.

entries.meaning: The science of substances and how they react with each other. ---
examples: Chemistry is my hardest class this semester.
He got an A in chemistry.
You need goggles for chemistry lab.

entries.meaning: The study of the earth's surface, its countries, and its features. ---
examples: American kids don't study much geography.
We had a geography quiz on the state capitals.
Geography is taught as part of social studies here.

entries.meaning: The study of basic questions about knowledge, existence, and right and wrong. ---
examples: He took philosophy to fill a requirement.
Philosophy majors read a lot.
She teaches ancient Greek philosophy.

entries.meaning: The study of the mind and how people behave. ---
examples: Psychology is one of the most popular majors.
She's taking intro to psychology this fall.
He wrote his paper on child psychology.
entries.contrast: The p is silent: sy-KAH-luh-jee.

entries.meaning: The study of human society and how groups of people behave. ---
examples: She switched from sociology to economics.
Sociology meets twice a week.
His sociology professor assigned three books.

entries.meaning: The study of human cultures and how people have lived. ---
examples: He teaches anthropology at a community college.
Anthropology took her to Peru for a summer.
I signed up for cultural anthropology.

entries.meaning: The study of designing and building machines, structures, and systems. ---
examples: She's studying electrical engineering.
The engineering building is across the quad.
Engineering is a five-year program there.

entries.meaning: The science of rocks and the structure of the earth. ---
examples: Geology students go on field trips every spring.
He took geology because it sounded easy.
Her geology class collected samples from the creek.

entries.meaning: The science of animals. ---
examples: She's finishing a degree in zoology.
Zoology was the only lab class that interested him.
The zoology department shares a building with biology.
entries.contrast: The first syllable rhymes with go, not with zoo: zoh-AH-luh-jee.

entries.meaning: The school subject about government and the duties of citizens. ---
examples: We learned how a bill becomes a law in civics.
Civics is required for graduation in this state.
His civics teacher made the class watch the debate.

entries.meaning: The American school subject combining history, geography, and government. ---
examples: Social studies is right after lunch.
We made posters about the fifty states in social studies.
Her favorite subject is social studies.
entries.contrast: Plural in form but singular in use: Social studies is my favorite class.

entries.meaning: The study of computers and how to program them. ---
examples: He's majoring in computer science.
The high school added a computer science class.
Computer science enrollment has doubled.

entries.meaning: The school subject of acting and putting on plays. ---
examples: She takes drama as an elective.
The drama teacher is directing the spring musical.
Drama club meets after school on Wednesdays.

entries.meaning: The writing of the correct letters of a word, or the ability to do it. ---
examples: Her spelling has improved a lot.
We have a spelling test every Friday.
Check your spelling before you turn it in.

entries.meaning: Basic math with numbers: adding, subtracting, multiplying, and dividing. ---
examples: Second graders practice simple arithmetic.
He made a mistake in the arithmetic.
You can do that arithmetic in your head.
entries.contrast: The noun is uh-RITH-muh-tik; the adjective in arithmetic mean shifts to a-rith-MET-ik.

entries.meaning: An area of knowledge studied at school, such as history or math. ---
examples: What's your favorite subject?
History is the one subject he really likes.
She's strong in all her subjects.
entries.contrast: Stress moves: the noun is SUB-jikt, the verb to subject is sub-JEKT.

entries.meaning: An important formal test of what a student has learned. ---
examples: The exam is on Thursday at nine.
He passed the exam on his second try.
Exams are worth half the grade.

entries.meaning: A set of questions used to measure what someone knows or can do. ---
examples: We have a test on chapter four tomorrow.
She studied all night for the test.
He aced both tests this week.

entries.meaning: A short test, usually on a small amount of material. ---
examples: There's a vocabulary quiz every Monday.
The quiz only took ten minutes.
He drops the two lowest quizzes.
entries.contrast: The plural doubles the z: quiz, quizzes.

entries.meaning: A short test given with no warning. ---
examples: She gave us a pop quiz on the reading.
Nobody was ready for the pop quiz.
He uses pop quizzes to make sure people do the homework.

entries.meaning: An exam given halfway through a course. ---
examples: The midterm covers everything through chapter seven.
I bombed the midterm but did well on the final.
Midterms start next week.

entries.meaning: The exam at the end of a course. ---
examples: My chemistry final is at eight in the morning.
Finals week is the worst week of the semester.
She skipped the party to study for finals.

entries.meaning: A letter or number showing how well a student did. ---
examples: She got a good grade on her essay.
My grades went up this semester.
He needs a passing grade to graduate.
entries.contrast: American grade where the British say mark; grade also means a school year, as in fifth grade, where the British say year or form.

entries.meaning: The number of points earned on a test. ---
examples: Her test score was in the top ten percent.
He raised his score by two hundred points.
The scores come back in three weeks.

entries.meaning: A written record of a student's grades sent home to parents. ---
examples: Report cards go out on Friday.
He hid his report card under the mattress.
There was one B on an otherwise perfect report card.

entries.meaning: An official record of all the courses a student took and the grades received. ---
examples: You have to send your transcript with the application.
The registrar mailed my transcript to three schools.
Official transcripts cost ten dollars each.

entries.meaning: A short piece of writing on one subject. ---
examples: The essay has to be five pages long.
I wrote my college essay about my grandmother.
He graded forty essays over the weekend.

entries.meaning: A long piece of writing assigned as the main work of a course. ---
examples: My term paper is due the last day of class.
She picked the Civil War for her term paper.
He put off both term papers until December.

entries.meaning: A short school paper describing a book a student has read. ---
examples: We had to write a book report over the break.
His book report was two pages long.
The class turned in book reports on Monday.

entries.meaning: A long piece of original research written for a doctoral degree. ---
examples: She's writing her dissertation on migrant workers.
His dissertation took six years.
The library keeps copies of old dissertations.

entries.meaning: What you say or write in reply to a question. ---
examples: Write your answer in the blank.
I knew the answer but forgot it during the test.
The answers are in the back of the book.
entries.contrast: The w is silent: AN-sur.

entries.meaning: A sentence that asks for information or an answer. ---
examples: Does anyone have a question?
I got the last question wrong.
The test had fifty multiple-choice questions.

entries.meaning: A chart showing exactly how an assignment will be graded. ---
examples: The rubric is posted on the class website.
Read the rubric before you start writing.
She grades every paper against the same rubric.

entries.meaning: A short plan listing the main points of a paper or talk in order. ---
examples: Turn in an outline before you write the paper.
Her outline was longer than my rough draft.
We compared outlines in study group.

entries.meaning: The fact of being present at school or class, or the number of people present. ---
examples: Attendance counts for ten percent of the grade.
The teacher takes attendance at the start of homeroom.
His attendance has been perfect all year.

entries.meaning: An occasion when someone is not at school or work. ---
examples: You need a note to excuse an absence.
Three unexcused absences mean a phone call home.
Her long absence put her behind in every class.

entries.meaning: An official document showing that someone has finished a course of study. ---
examples: He framed his high school diploma.
You need a diploma to apply for most jobs.
The diplomas were handed out one by one.

entries.meaning: An official paper stating that someone has completed training or met a standard. ---
examples: She earned a certificate in medical billing.
The program gives you a certificate, not a degree.
He hung both certificates behind his desk.

entries.meaning: The first degree earned at a college, usually after four years. ---
examples: The job requires a bachelor's degree.
She finished her bachelor's degree at night.
Both of their bachelor's degrees are in nursing.

entries.meaning: A degree earned after a bachelor's degree, usually in one or two years. ---
examples: He's working on a master's degree in education.
A master's degree means a pay raise in this district.
She has two master's degrees.

entries.meaning: The highest university degree, earned by doing original research. ---
examples: She earned her doctorate in linguistics.
A doctorate usually takes five or six years.
The department awarded four doctorates this spring.

entries.meaning: The main subject a college student studies for a degree. ---
examples: What's your major?
She changed her major twice.
Engineering and nursing are the most popular majors here.

entries.meaning: A second, smaller field of study alongside a college major. ---
examples: He's got a minor in Spanish.
A minor takes about six classes.
The college offers over forty minors.
entries.contrast: Sounds exactly like miner, someone who digs in a mine.

entries.meaning: Special recognition for excellent grades, or the advanced version of a class. ---
examples: She graduated with honors.
He's in honors English this year.
The department awards honors to the top ten percent.
entries.contrast: The h is silent: AH-nurz. The British spell it honours.

entries.meaning: Money given to a student to pay for school, usually for good grades or need. ---
examples: He got a full scholarship to play baseball.
She's applying for every scholarship she can find.
The scholarship covers tuition but not housing.

entries.meaning: Money awarded to a graduate student or researcher to support their work. ---
examples: The fellowship pays for two years of research.
She won a teaching fellowship.
Only three fellowships are awarded each year.

entries.meaning: The money paid to a school or college for teaching. ---
examples: Tuition went up again this year.
His parents pay half his tuition.
Out-of-state tuition is nearly double.
entries.contrast: In the US tuition means the fees you pay; in Britain it means the teaching itself.

entries.meaning: The right to enter a school or college as a student. ---
examples: She was offered admission to her first-choice school.
Admission to the program is competitive.
He's waiting to hear about admission.

entries.meaning: The act of signing up for school, or the number of students signed up. ---
examples: Enrollment is down at the community college.
Enrollment for fall classes opens Monday.
The school has an enrollment of about nine hundred.
entries.contrast: Americans double the l: enrollment; the British write enrolment.

entries.meaning: The ceremony where students receive their degrees or diplomas. ---
examples: My whole family came to graduation.
Graduation is the second Saturday in June.
She's been to three graduations this month.

entries.meaning: The formal graduation ceremony at an American school or college. ---
examples: The governor gave the commencement speech.
Commencement is held on the football field.
Rain moved both commencements indoors.
entries.contrast: In American schools commencement means graduation, even though the word literally means a beginning.

entries.meaning: A class you must finish before you are allowed to take another one. ---
examples: Algebra is a prerequisite for chemistry.
She hasn't met the prerequisite yet.
I spent my first year knocking out prerequisites.

entries.meaning: A class a student chooses rather than one that is required. ---
examples: I took photography as an elective.
You need three electives to graduate.
The elective filled up in an hour.

entries.meaning: Money borrowed to pay for college that must be paid back later. ---
examples: She's still paying off her student loans.
He took out a student loan for his last two years.
Congress voted to lower the interest on student loans.

entries.meaning: A meeting of the whole school in one room. ---
examples: There's an assembly in the gym this afternoon.
The principal announced it at assembly.
We only have two or three assemblies a year.

entries.meaning: A punishment where a student must stay at school after class. ---
examples: He got detention for talking back.
Detention is in room 204 until four o'clock.
Three detentions mean a call to your parents.

entries.meaning: A punishment in which a student is banned from school for a short time. ---
examples: The fight earned him a three-day suspension.
She's appealing the suspension.
Suspensions have dropped since the new policy.

entries.meaning: The sound that marks the beginning and end of a class period. ---
examples: The bell rang before I finished the last question.
Stay seated until the bell.
The bells are two minutes fast.

entries.meaning: A school outing where students visit a place to learn about it. ---
examples: We're going on a field trip to the aquarium.
Your parents have to sign a permission slip for the field trip.
The class takes two field trips a year.

entries.meaning: A period during the school day set aside for quiet studying. ---
examples: I do my homework in study hall.
He has study hall sixth period.
The library is used for study halls in the morning.

entries.meaning: The week off from school in the spring. ---
examples: We drove to Florida over spring break.
Spring break is the third week of March.
They booked a beach house for spring break.

entries.meaning: Classes held during the summer, often to make up a failed course. ---
examples: He has to go to summer school for geometry.
Summer school runs from June to early August.
The district cut two of its summer schools.

entries.meaning: A formal dance for high school students, usually in the spring. ---
examples: He asked her to prom in the cafeteria.
Prom is at a hotel downtown this year.
She went to three proms in high school.

entries.meaning: A book published each year with photos of the students and school events. ---
examples: Everyone signed my yearbook on the last day.
My yearbook photo is awful.
She kept all four of her high school yearbooks.

entries.meaning: A group of students who meet regularly to share an interest. ---
examples: She joined the chess club.
The Spanish club meets on Tuesdays.
Colleges like to see that you joined clubs.

entries.meaning: Control over behavior, kept by rules and punishment. ---
examples: The new principal is stricter about discipline.
There's no discipline in that classroom.
Discipline problems dropped after the rule changed.

entries.meaning: A period of teaching on one topic. ---
examples: Today's lesson is about fractions.
She takes piano lessons on Saturdays.
The lesson ran ten minutes long.
entries.contrast: Sounds exactly like lessen, the verb meaning to reduce.

entries.meaning: The subject that something is written or spoken about. ---
examples: Pick a topic for your research paper.
That topic comes up again in chapter nine.
We covered three topics in one class.

entries.meaning: One of the numbered parts a book is divided into. ---
examples: Read chapter six for Thursday.
The test covers the first four chapters.
Each chapter ends with review questions.

entries.meaning: A book used for studying a subject in class. ---
examples: The biology textbook weighs a ton.
I bought my textbooks used.
The textbook is online this year.

entries.meaning: A book of exercises that students write their answers in. ---
examples: Do page twelve in your workbook.
She finished the whole workbook by March.
The workbooks come with the textbook.

entries.meaning: A printed page of problems or questions for students to fill in. ---
examples: Pass the worksheet back when you're done.
He lost the worksheet on the bus.
She copied thirty worksheets before class.

entries.meaning: A printed sheet given to everyone in a class or meeting. ---
examples: The handout has the formulas on it.
Grab a handout on your way in.
All the handouts are posted online too.

entries.meaning: A small card with a question on one side and the answer on the other. ---
examples: I made flashcards for the vocabulary test.
She quizzed him with flashcards in the car.
One flashcard fell behind the couch.

entries.meaning: A small zippered bag or box for holding pens and pencils. ---
examples: Her pencil case is stuffed with markers.
He dumped out his pencil case looking for an eraser.
The store had pencil cases on sale.

entries.meaning: A device that cuts a point on the end of a pencil. ---
examples: The pencil sharpener is by the door.
He broke the pencil sharpener on the first day.
Every classroom has two pencil sharpeners.

entries.meaning: A small machine that does arithmetic. ---
examples: No calculators on this part of the test.
My graphing calculator cost a hundred dollars.
He left his calculator in his locker.

entries.meaning: A book or app listing words with their meanings. ---
examples: Look it up in the dictionary.
There's a beat-up dictionary on every desk.
The library keeps dictionaries in six languages.

entries.meaning: A book or website with articles on many subjects, arranged alphabetically. ---
examples: We used an encyclopedia for our reports back then.
Teachers don't accept an online encyclopedia as a source.
Old encyclopedias still line the back shelf.

entries.meaning: A book of maps. ---
examples: Find Peru in the atlas.
The atlas is older than I am.
Two atlases were missing from the shelf.

entries.meaning: A drawing of an area showing where places are. ---
examples: There's a map of the country on the wall.
We had to label the rivers on a blank map.
Old maps still hang in the geography room.

entries.meaning: A small container a child carries food to school in. ---
examples: He forgot his lunchbox on the counter.
There's an apple at the bottom of her lunchbox.
The lunchboxes go on the shelf by the door.

entries.meaning: A small device blown to make a loud sound, used to get attention. ---
examples: The gym teacher blew his whistle.
She wears a whistle around her neck at recess.
You could hear the whistles from the field.
entries.contrast: The t is silent: WISS-uhl.

entries.meaning: An instrument that makes very small things look much larger. ---
examples: Look at the cells under the microscope.
He adjusted the microscope until the slide came into focus.
The lab has twelve microscopes.

entries.meaning: A thin glass tube used to hold liquids in a science lab. ---
examples: Pour the solution into the test tube.
He dropped a test tube and had to sweep up the glass.
Each pair got three test tubes and a rack.

entries.meaning: Something written down so it can be remembered later. ---
examples: I took notes during the whole lecture.
Can I borrow your notes from Tuesday?
She scribbled a note in the margin.

entries.meaning: The process of teaching and learning, especially in schools. ---
examples: She wants a better education for her kids.
He never finished his education.
Education takes up a third of the state budget.

entries.meaning: The process of gaining knowledge or skill. ---
examples: Learning a language takes years.
The noise makes learning almost impossible.
Kids do a lot of their learning through play.

entries.meaning: A long talk given to teach a group of students. ---
examples: The lecture lasted fifty minutes.
I fell asleep during the lecture.
His lectures are posted as videos.

entries.meaning: A small class where students discuss a subject with a teacher. ---
examples: The seminar has only twelve students.
Everyone has to present once in the seminar.
She teaches two graduate seminars.

entries.meaning: The work students do for a class during the term, apart from exams. ---
examples: Half the grade comes from coursework.
He finished his coursework but not his thesis.
The coursework is heavier than I expected.
entries.contrast: Uncountable: say a lot of coursework or three assignments, never three courseworks.

entries.meaning: A talk in which people share ideas about a subject. ---
examples: The discussion got heated near the end.
Class discussion counts toward your grade.
We had long discussions about the ending of the book.

entries.meaning: A formal argument in which two sides give opposing views. ---
examples: She joined the debate team her sophomore year.
The debate was about school uniforms.
They won three debates in a row.

entries.meaning: A scientific test done to find out or prove something. ---
examples: We did an experiment with vinegar and baking soda.
Write up the experiment for Friday.
The experiments are graded on the lab report.

entries.meaning: An explanation of something that is supported by evidence and reasoning. ---
examples: We spent a week on the theory of evolution.
That's just a theory, not a proven fact.
Competing theories are covered in chapter eight.

entries.meaning: A general idea about how something works. ---
examples: The concept of gravity is introduced early.
She grasped the concept right away.
The chapter covers three basic concepts.

entries.meaning: A statement of what a word or term means. ---
examples: Copy the definition into your notebook.
The test asks for the definition of photosynthesis.
We had to memorize twenty definitions.

entries.meaning: A list of the books and articles used in a piece of writing. ---
examples: The paper needs a bibliography at the end.
Her bibliography runs four pages.
He forgot to alphabetize both bibliographies.

entries.meaning: A note in a paper showing where a fact or quotation came from. ---
examples: Every quote needs a citation.
He lost points for a sloppy citation.
The professor checks the citations carefully.

entries.meaning: A note at the bottom of a page explaining something in the text. ---
examples: The explanation is in a footnote.
Put the source in a footnote, not in the paragraph.
The chapter has ninety footnotes.

entries.meaning: The act of using someone else's words or ideas as if they were your own. ---
examples: Plagiarism can get you expelled.
The school runs every paper through plagiarism software.
He was accused of plagiarism and failed the course.

entries.meaning: Doing something over and over in order to get better at it. ---
examples: It takes practice to get good at fractions.
With enough practice, the times tables come easily.
She needs more practice before the recital.
entries.contrast: Americans spell the noun and the verb the same way; the British write the noun practice and the verb practise.

entries.meaning: The desire that makes someone want to work at something. ---
examples: He has the ability but no motivation.
Motivation drops off in the last week of the semester.
Good grades gave her the motivation to keep going.

entries.meaning: Something difficult that someone has succeeded in doing.
examples: Finishing the degree while working was a real achievement.
The school honors academic achievement every spring.
Her achievements filled half the application.
